claims.text: The initial materials are nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as homogeneous single-phase solid solutions.
Sluggish atomic diffusion is the predominant governor of structural and chemical stability across 473–1923 K.
Diffusion in smaller nanoparticles is especially surface-mediated.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio than larger nanoparticles.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio increases effective surface diffusion rates at elevated temperature.
Atomic mobility increases at elevated temperatures.
High mixing entropy alone cannot necessarily prevent phase segregation or chemical reordering.
These multimetallic systems can have a thermodynamic drive toward chemical reordering or phase decomposition.
Larger nanoparticles exhibit sluggish diffusion that kinetically traps atoms in their initial configuration.
Under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions, larger nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous single-phase solid solution better than smaller nanoparticles.
Under otherwise identical high-temperature conditions, smaller nanoparticles will show more phase segregation or chemical reordering because of enhanced surface diffusion.
Nanoparticle size can be varied while composition, atmosphere, external stress, and initial phase state are held constant.
Composition and temperature can affect decomposition or chemical ordering independently of particle size.
The size threshold separating bulk-like sluggish diffusion from substantial surface diffusion is unknown and may vary with composition or environment.
In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy with EDS, and diffusion measurements can distinguish phase stability, chemical homogeneity, and atomic mobility between size groups.
Comparable stability in both size groups, or no greater segregation or reordering in smaller particles, would falsify the proposed size-governed kinetic mechanism.
